title: Agentic AI for Scientific Reasoning in Autonomous Quantum Sensing Experiments
authors: Takuya Isogawa, Ryotaro Okabe, Nutdech Phadetsuwannukun, Mingda Li, Paola Cappellaro
abstract: We implement an agentic AI workflow built around a large language model (LLM) agent for autonomous experiments with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. NV centers are a widely used platform for quantum sensing, and the ability to control many measurements from a computer makes NV experiments a natural setting for autonomous workflows. We make two main contributions. First, we demonstrate an autonomous NV experiment workflow that combines persistent project records, quantitative calculation and data analysis tools, and deterministic experiment control. In one autonomous experiment, the agent selected a single NV center, calibrated its resonant frequency, measured \(T_2^\ast\) with Ramsey measurements, and added a Carr--Purcell--Meiboom--Gill (CPMG) measurement to check a weak feature that could be related to nearby \(^{13}\mathrm{C}\). Second, we introduce two offline benchmarks that evaluate the agent's reasoning separately from laboratory execution. We evaluated both benchmarks with GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol. In the Ramsey checkpoint benchmark, greater reasoning effort generally improved recognition of a residual resonance calibration offset. By contrast, in the pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance (pODMR) data evaluation benchmark, pulse sequence information alone produced more false positive resonance judgments at higher reasoning effort. Requiring an expected signal calculation kept false positive rates low across all three models and reasoning settings. The results suggest a clear division of labor for autonomous experiments. The agent forms scientific hypotheses and uses quantitative tools to evaluate data, while deterministic code controls the hardware and enforces safety constraints.
summary: The paper introduces an agentic AI framework that allows autonomous execution of complex quantum sensing experiments using NV centers. The system uses LLMs to hypothesize next steps and interpret data from measurements like pODMR scans, successfully designing follow-up tests (like CPMG) based on initial weak signals. It establishes a clear division of labor where the AI handles scientific reasoning while deterministic code manages hardware safety.
main_problem: Developing autonomous experimental workflows for quantum sensing that can handle complex decision-making, data interpretation, and hypothesis generation beyond routine hardware control.
main_result: The agent successfully performed an end-to-end workflow—from initial measurement to autonomously designing a follow-up CPMG scan—and benchmarks show that the division of labor between LLM reasoning and deterministic code is crucial for success.
method: An agentic AI workflow built around a Large Language Model (LLM) guides autonomous experiments, combining persistent state tracking with quantitative tools to interpret complex quantum measurement data.
model_or_system: The physical system is Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, used for sensing magnetic and electric fields via pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance (pODMR) and Ramsey measurements. The AI component uses LLMs (e.g., GPT variants) to reason over the experimental process.
key_observables: T2* decay time, resonance frequencies, signal depth in pODMR data, and detection of weak frequency components related to nearby ${}^{13}	ext{C}$ coupling.
important_parameters: Reasoning effort levels (Low to X-high), contrast depth thresholds ($\geq 0.132$), and specific microwave/Larmor frequencies (e.g., $3.87650 	ext{ GHz}$).
main_assumptions: The agent's ability to form hypotheses is tested against deterministic hardware control, but the use of specific thresholds in retrospective analysis may not generalize.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the sequence of autonomous measurements (Ramsey $ightarrow$ CPMG) and benchmark comparisons showing model performance across varying reasoning efforts for both Ramsey checkpoint tasks and pODMR data evaluation.
paper_structure: The paper details an autonomous workflow on NV centers, presents case studies demonstrating hypothesis-driven measurement design (e.g., adding CPMG), and rigorously evaluates the LLM's reasoning capabilities using two distinct offline benchmarks (Ramsey checkpoint and pODMR).
why_interesting: This work represents a significant step toward closing the loop in quantum experiments by integrating advanced AI reasoning directly into the experimental control cycle, which is highly relevant for complex open quantum systems characterization.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the autonomous NV experiment workflow. The human researcher gives an experimental objective to the LLM agent. The agent uses project records, memory and knowledge documents, and quantitative analysis tools on the agent computer. It submits jobs through a shared folder and receives recorded data from the experiment system. On the experiment computer, deterministic software manages the queue, verifies requests and safety conditions, executes accepted jobs, controls the hardware, and records data. The agent has no direct access to the hardware.

Figure 2. Autonomous workflow demonstration from the main experiment. Panel (a) shows the main experimental stages as exchanges between the agent and the experiment system. Panel (b) shows the new image scan. Panels (c) and (d) show strong-π pODMR measurements for the rejected and selected candidates. Panel (e) shows the weak-π pODMR resonance calibration. Panel (f) shows one representative Ramsey measurement, and panel (g) shows the autonomous CPMG N = 8 check of the weak 13C-like feature.

Figure 3. Ramsey checkpoint benchmark across three models. Panel (a) illustrates hypothesis formation from project records and returned data. Panel (b) shows aggregate pass rates over five checkpoints and twenty replicates per checkpoint for GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol at each reasoning effort. Labels give passing runs out of 100. Panels (c), (d), and (e) show checkpoint level pass counts for GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol, respectively. A pass requires the response to connect a residual Ramsey frequency offset to resonance frequency or microwave frequency calibration. Each heat map cell is the number of passing runs out of twenty replicates.

Figure 4. pODMR benchmark across three models. Panel (a) illustrates how calculations and simulations guide pODMR data evaluation, with representative measurements without and with a resonance. Panels (b), (c), and (d) show the false positive rate for the sequence, domain facts, and expected signal conditions, respectively. Panels (e), (f), and (g) show the corresponding overall classification accuracy. Each point pools three replicates of the same 96 measurements. Error bars show measurement level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

NV sensing of materials.note: The new paper explicitly uses Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond for sensing magnetic and electric fields via pODMR and Ramsey measurements, directly matching the core subject matter.
